article.title: How to Screen and Recoat Hardwood Floors
article.summary: Refresh dull, lightly scratched hardwood without sanding: check the finish, deep-clean, abrade with a screen, then roll on new polyurethane.
article.body:
Screening and recoating lightly abrades the existing finish and adds a fresh coat of polyurethane on top. It brings back the shine and protection for a fraction of the cost of full sanding. It works when the wear is in the finish, not into the wood.

Safety: ventilate well and follow the finish label. A rental buffer can jerk sideways when you start it: keep it level and hold on with both hands. Rags with oil-based finish can catch fire on their own: lay them flat to dry outdoors.

Steps

  1. Check that the floor is a candidate

    Screen and recoat works on floors with an intact polyurethane finish and surface scratches. It won't fix gray, worn-through spots, deep gouges, or water stains in the wood, which need sanding. If the floor was waxed or treated with a polish, a new finish won't stick: drop a little water on it; if white spots appear after a few minutes, there may be wax.

    Done right: the wear is in the finish only and the floor has no wax.

  2. Empty the room and deep-clean

    Remove everything, including floor vents. Vacuum, then clean with a hardwood floor cleaner, not a soap or oil product. Let it dry.

    Done right: the floor is clean, dry and free of grit.

  3. Abrade the finish

    Run a buffer with a screen pad over the floor in overlapping passes, moving with the grain. Hand-sand the edges and corners the buffer can't reach. You're only dulling the finish so the new coat sticks, not removing it.

    Done right: the whole floor looks evenly dull, with no shiny spots left.

  4. Remove every bit of dust

    Vacuum thoroughly, including gaps between boards, then wipe the floor with a slightly damp microfiber tack pad. Dust left behind ends up in the finish.

    Done right: a dark cloth wiped across the floor picks up no dust.

  5. Roll on the new finish

    Starting at the far wall and working toward the exit, cut in a band along the edges, then apply a thin, even coat with an applicator pad or roller, keeping a wet edge and following the grain. Apply a second coat after the recoat time on the can, if the product calls for it.

    Done right: the finish is even, with no puddles, lap marks or missed spots.

  6. Let it cure

    Walk on it in socks only after the time on the label. Wait longer before bringing back furniture, and at least a week or as the label says before putting rugs down. Use felt pads under furniture legs.

    Done right: the floor has an even sheen and no tacky spots.

Hire a flooring refinisher if: the finish is worn through to bare wood, the floor has deep scratches or pet stains, you're changing the color, or the floor is engineered with a thin wear layer.

FAQ

What is screen and recoat?

It means lightly abrading the existing floor finish and applying a fresh coat of polyurethane, without sanding down to bare wood.

How often should hardwood floors be recoated?

Often every 3 to 5 years in busy homes, before the finish wears through.

Can you recoat a floor with scratches?

Surface scratches in the finish usually disappear. Scratches into the wood need sanding.

Can you recoat a waxed floor?

Not with polyurethane. The wax must be removed first, which usually means professional sanding.
